summary: CDAS proposes a plausible, interpretability-motivated alternative to Lang./PO steering by combining a JSD distribution-matching objective with distributed interchange interventions, and the safety case studies credibly show better utility preservation than strong-supervised RePS. However, the paper’s core narrative of more faithful, causally grounded, (near) tuning-free control is only partially supported: AXBENCH gains are mixed and layer-sensitive, unit-factor CDAS underperforms badly, and the two claimed ingredients (JSD objective vs. DII protocol) are not cleanly ablated. As submitted, this is a promising but incomplete ICLR contribution that needs stronger causal isolation of design choices and broader, more consistent evidence before acceptance.
strengths: Clear conceptual framing that ties intervention-based steering to causal-feature localization rather than preference/likelihood fine-tuning proxies.
Method is coherent: bi-directional DII plus full-vocabulary JSD matching is a genuine alternative supervision signal to Lang./PO.
Safety case studies (refusal override up to 70B; CoT backdoor neutralization) provide the paper’s strongest evidence, especially utility/KL preservation versus RePS.
Calibration is relatively honest: mixed AXBENCH outcomes, layer sensitivity, and limitations (data requirements, factor tuning, rank-1 scope, weak causal grounding) are stated rather than buried.

key_concerns.issue: The two claimed contributions—JSD distribution matching and DII—are not isolated with adequate ablations. The ‘DAS’ baseline replaces only the objective with Lang. under DII, but there is no JSD+addition (or JSD vs KL/other divergences) comparison, nor a controlled test of whether bi-directional gains come from D+/D−, clamping, or the counterfactual factor distribution.
key_concerns.suggested_fix: Add a factorial ablation (objective × intervention protocol × factor source) on at least one AXBENCH setting and one case study, with matched data/compute and the same inference protocol.

key_concerns.issue: The faithfulness/tuning-free story is undermined by AXBENCH: unit-factor CDAS is weak, tuned β≫1 is required for competitiveness, and results remain inconsistent across layers/models versus RePS/Lang.
key_concerns.suggested_fix: Either deliver a principled tuning-free inference rule that works, or reframe claims around utility-preserving suppression; report full factor-sensitivity curves and fair-selection variance for all methods.

key_concerns.issue: Experimental breadth and statistical reporting are uneven for the generality implied by ‘general-purpose steering’: AXBENCH is Gemma-only, rank-1 only, layer choices are sparse/grid-searched differently per setting, and multi-seed/error bars are clear mainly for the backdoor ASR figure.
key_concerns.suggested_fix: Add another model family, report seeds/intervals for refusal and AXBENCH primary metrics, and standardize layer/factor selection protocols across methods.

key_concerns.issue: Naming the Lang.+DII baseline ‘DAS’ collides with the established DAS localization method and makes positioning harder to parse.
key_concerns.suggested_fix: Rename the baseline (e.g., Lang-DII) and keep ‘DAS’ only for the prior localization method.

key_concerns.issue: Training-data construction (gpt-4o-mini neutral responses / template x→xc; red-team augmentation) could confound comparisons if baselines are not identically constrained.
key_concerns.suggested_fix: State and, where possible, equalize data access for all optimization-based methods; ablate synthetic-augmentation quality.

questions_for_authors: If unit-factor DII is the ‘principled’ inference choice, why is β-tuning necessary for AXBENCH, and what does that imply for the claim that source-induced factors stay on-distribution?
Does replacing JSD with forward/reverse KL or a token-level CE-to-teacher distribution recover most gains under the same DII protocol?
Can CDAS with addition interventions (no DII) match clamping/DII performance, holding the JSD objective fixed?
For refusal and AXBENCH, what is seed-to-seed variance of steering vectors and scores under identical hyperparameters?
How sensitive are conclusions to the chosen <model>-span token for one-to-many DII, beyond the reported grid search?
calibration_check: Claims are partly well-scoped in the conclusion, but the title/intro still oversell ‘faithful’ bi-directional steering relative to mixed AXBENCH results and dependence on inference-time factor scaling.

significance.justification: Steering-plus-interpretability is timely and the utility-preserving suppression angle would interest ICLR readers, but impact is tempered by inconsistent primary benchmark wins.

novelty.justification: JSD matching with DII for bi-directional steering is a meaningful twist on DAS/RePS-era work, yet remains an incremental combination rather than a sharply new paradigm.

rigor.justification: Method derivation is coherent and case-study controls are thoughtful, but missing component ablations and factor-tuning confounds weaken the claim–evidence link.

statistical_soundness.justification: Fair splits on AXBENCH and 3-seed ASR with SE help, but refusal/AXBENCH primary tables lack consistent multi-seed intervals and formal significance testing.

calibration_honesty.justification: Limitations and non-dominance versus Lang./PO are acknowledged, though branding as broadly ‘faithful’ still outruns the mixed evidence.

clarity.justification: Overall organization is readable and equations are usable, but dense notation and the DAS/CDAS/DAS-baseline naming overload reduce precision.

structure_compliance.justification: Standard ICLR flow (intro, related work, method, benchmark, case studies, conclusion/limitations) is present and appropriately scoped in length.

reproducibility.justification: Data construction, DII protocol, objectives, and inference factor rules are described sufficiently in principle; some hyperparameter/appendix details remain thin in the body.

related_work.justification: Positioning against Lang./PO steering, DAS/DII localization, and refusal/backdoor probing literature is fair and current within the prose.

figure_quality.justification: Captions for Tables 1–4 and Figure 1 clearly state comparisons and support the main claims, though AXBENCH presentation is dense and oracle-vs-fair results need careful reading.

breadth_generality.justification: Evidence is narrow relative to claimed generality: Gemma-only AXBENCH, rank-1 only, sparse layers, and no ablations that would justify broad methodological conclusions.

overall_recommendation.justification: Promising idea with credible safety-case upside, but missing ablations and inconsistent/tuned general-purpose results place it at borderline reject for ICLR 2026 as submitted.
